Generic Cantor actions of Z wr Z are hyperfinite

By Alec Kriebel, independent researcher.
Manuscript dated 13 October 2026 · Version 1.0.0 · Unrefereed preprint

Read the paper (PDF, 5 pages) · Source and verification materials (ZIP) · Zenodo record

Plain-English explanation · Read on this page · Collaboration

Abstract

We give an affirmative answer to Question 3 in Iyer's contribution, joint with Shinko, to Oberwolfach Report 2/2025. A dense Gδ of continuous actions of the restricted wreath product ℤ ≀ ℤ on Cantor space has hyperfinite orbit equivalence relation on the entire space. We specialize established Cantor-action lifting principles to obtain a continuous profinite shift height. Finite-width lamp slabs then satisfy the compatible-metric theorem of Conley–Jackson–Marks–Seward–Tucker-Drob. The full preimage of the embedded integers is treated by a separate finite Borel exhaustion. The auxiliary Borel theorem requires the height factor and allows stabilizers.

The idea in plain English

A group action describes how transformations move points. Two points lie in the same orbit when one can be moved to the other. Hyperfiniteness means that this orbit relation can be built from an increasing sequence of Borel equivalence relations whose classes are finite.

The group here is the restricted wreath product ℤ ≀ ℤ: an integer shift acts on finitely supported configurations of integer-valued lamps. The paper shows that a generic continuous action on Cantor space has a hyperfinite orbit relation on the whole space. Generic refers to Baire category in the space of all these actions, rather than a probability estimate.

The proof constructs compatible height coordinates modulo successively larger factorials. It cuts the action into finite-width slabs and applies established results on Borel asymptotic dimension. A separate construction handles every point whose profinite height is an ordinary integer.

The precise result

Let W=(⊕ᵢ∈ℤ ℤ)⋊ℤ be the countable discrete restricted wreath product. There is a dense Gδ subset of the full Polish space Act(W,2^ℕ) of continuous actions, with the subspace topology from Homeo(2^ℕ)^W and compact-open homeomorphism topologies, such that every action in this subset has a hyperfinite orbit equivalence relation on the entire Cantor space 2^ℕ.

More generally, suppose W acts Borelly on a standard Borel space X and admits an actual Borel map p:X→Ẑ satisfying p(gx)=p(x)+χ(g), where χ:W→ℤ is the shift homomorphism and Ẑ=lim ℤ/n!ℤ is the group of profinite integers. Then its orbit equivalence relation is hyperfinite on all of X. The theorem permits stabilizers and does not require freeness, minimality, an invariant probability measure or surjectivity of p.

The main theorem answers Question 3 in Iyer’s contribution, joint with Shinko, to Oberwolfach Report 2/2025. This is the historically posed whole-space generic-action question. The auxiliary Borel result requires the height factor; it does not establish hyperfiniteness for every Borel W-action.

Why the result holds

The paper specializes established Cantor-action lifting principles. A direct construction gives compatible height maps modulo successive factorials, using countably many open dense extension conditions in the full action space. Their inverse limit is a continuous equivariant height map; in this compact Cantor setting it is onto.

At each fixed slab width, the lamp directions form a finite-rank free abelian group. Deep results of Conley, Jackson, Marks, Seward and Tucker-Drob give finite Borel asymptotic dimension for its action, including actions with stabilizers. The dimension may grow with the width, and slab components may be infinite. Divisible widths give nested slab graphs with decreasing distances, supplying the exact compatible-metric hypothesis of their Theorem 7.3.

On the full preimage of the embedded integers, which may be uncountable, the proof normalizes to height zero. It combines a finite Borel exhaustion for the lamp subgroup with increasing bounded intervals of integer heights. The height cutoff is essential to keep the pulled-back classes finite. The regular and exceptional pieces are invariant and their finite exhaustions can then be combined.

Scope and limitations

Genericity concerns a dense Gδ subset of the full space of continuous Cantor actions. Hyperfiniteness holds on every point of the phase space for those actions. The statement does not merely discard a null or meager subset of points, and it does not identify the entire set of hyperfinite actions as Gδ.

The general Borel theorem assumes an actual equivariant profinite height map. Stabilizers and nonsurjective maps are allowed. The onto height obtained for generic continuous Cantor actions is a consequence of that compact setting, rather than an added assumption in the Borel theorem. The paper does not treat all Borel W-actions without a height factor.

Finite Borel asymptotic dimension of each slab does not mean that its orbit components are finite. Dimension bounds need not be uniform across widths. The proof uses a specific compatible-metric theorem, rather than a general theorem about increasing unions of hyperfinite relations.

The proof relies on deep prior Borel theorems. Finite diagnostics in the supporting materials check local group and slab behavior; they do not prove the Baire-category or infinite Borel assertions. No comeager conjugacy class, uniform Borel choice of heights or exhaustions across actions, or clopen finite exhaustion is claimed.

Deep derived pure braids need not be 1-solvable

By Alec Kriebel, independent researcher.
Manuscript dated 15 October 2026 · Version 1.0 · Unrefereed preprint

Read the paper (PDF, 4 pages) · Source and verification package (ZIP) · Zenodo record

Plain-English explanation · Read on this page · Collaboration

Abstract

For every m≥3 and every finite k≥1, the kth ordinary derived subgroup of the pure braid group contains a braid whose standard closure is not integrally smoothly 1-solvable. Consequently P_m^{(n+2)}⊄F_n^m for every integer n≥1, answering negatively the derived-series containment question in the Harvey–Park–Ray Oberwolfach contribution. The proof combines established signature-quasimorphism results with amenable-quotient rigidity and a pointwise signature obstruction to 1-solvability. The general quasimorphism ingredients are prior results. An accompanying exact verification package also preserves an explicit 104-crossing example in P_3^{(3)}.

The idea in plain English

Pure braids return each strand to its starting position. Repeatedly taking commutators creates the derived series, an increasingly restrictive sequence of subgroups. A separate notion, called 1-solvability, asks whether the closed braid fits into a four-dimensional construction with specified surfaces and intersection properties.

The paper shows that for every number of strands at least three, a braid can lie arbitrarily far down the derived series and still fail 1-solvability. For each finite depth there is a witness; the argument does not use one braid that works simultaneously at every depth.

The general argument connects established results about braid signatures and quasimorphisms. The supporting materials also give a concrete three-strand word with 104 crossings at the third derived level. That finite example illustrates one case of the broader existence theorem.

The precise result

Let P_m be the classical disk pure braid group, with P_m^(0)=P_m and P_m^(k+1)=[P_m^(k),P_m^(k)]. For every m≥3 and every finite integer k≥1, some braid in P_m^(k) has standard oriented closure that is not integrally smoothly 1-solvable in the sense of Otto Definition 2.3.

Equivalently, the string-link concordance classes represented by P_m^(k) are not all in F₁^m. Since F_n^m⊂F₁^m for integers n≥1, this gives P_m^(n+2)⊄F_n^m for every m≥3 and integer n≥1, a negative answer to Question 3 in the Harvey–Park–Ray Oberwolfach contribution.

For the explicit third-derived example, set a=σ₁², b=σ₂², c=[a,b], d=a⁻¹ca, e=b⁻¹cb, u=[c,d], v=[d,e] and β=[u,v], using [x,y]=xyx⁻¹y⁻¹. The paper gives a 104-letter freely reduced Artin word for β with closure signature −2.

Why the result holds

The ordinary signature s of a three-strand braid closure has bounded failure of additivity. Its homogenization q is a homogeneous quasimorphism, exactly linear on powers. Published signature formulas show that q restricted to the pure braid group P₃ is not a homomorphism.

A nonhomomorphic homogeneous quasimorphism cannot vanish on a finite derived subgroup. Otherwise it would descend to a solvable, hence amenable, quotient, where homogeneous quasimorphisms are homomorphisms. The general ingredients are established results.

The ordinary signature and its homogenization are distinct. A suitable positive power is essential: nonzero q on a braid does not by itself give nonzero ordinary signature on that same braid. The powered braid has nonzero ordinary signature and zero pairwise linking numbers. A pointwise signature obstruction rules out an integral smooth 1-solution; adding split trivial strands reaches every m≥3.

Scope and limitations

The result uses the ordinary derived series of classical disk pure braid groups and integral smooth solvability of standard closures. It makes no claim for power subgroups, lower central series, rational derived series, surface braid groups, rational solvability or a merely topological solvability category.

The witness may depend on the finite depth k. No single braid in the intersection of all derived subgroups is asserted, and the explicit 104-crossing word is supplied only for k=3. No minimal crossing number or effective word-length bound at arbitrary depth is claimed.

For m=1 and m=2, the positive derived subgroups are trivial. The consequence for the solvable filtration is stated for integers n≥1; it does not contradict the prior n=0 containment discussed in the original report.

The general signature, quasimorphism and amenable-group tools are credited prior results. The contribution presented is their application to this particular containment question, together with the explicit finite example. No historical firstness, exhaustive novelty clearance or continued worldwide openness is claimed.

For the separate explicit example, the supporting derivation reconstructs the Goeritz form from crossing geometry and records a printed index discrepancy in Erle’s matrix formula. A separate Burau–Meyer calculation gives the same signature. This qualification concerns the finite example; the arbitrary-depth existence proof is independent of that calculation.

Abstract

For every m≥3 and every finite k≥1, the kth ordinary derived subgroup of the pure braid group contains a braid whose standard closure is not integrally smoothly 1-solvable. Consequently P_m^{(n+2)}⊄F_n^m for every integer n≥1, answering negatively the derived-series containment question in the Harvey–Park–Ray Oberwolfach contribution. The proof combines established signature-quasimorphism results with amenable-quotient rigidity and a pointwise signature obstruction to 1-solvability. The general quasimorphism ingredients are prior results. An accompanying exact verification package also preserves an explicit 104-crossing example in P_3^{(3)}.

The idea in plain English

Pure braids return each strand to its starting position. Repeatedly taking commutators creates the derived series, an increasingly restrictive sequence of subgroups. A separate notion, called 1-solvability, asks whether the closed braid fits into a four-dimensional construction with specified surfaces and intersection properties.

The paper shows that for every number of strands at least three, a braid can lie arbitrarily far down the derived series and still fail 1-solvability. For each finite depth there is a witness; the argument does not use one braid that works simultaneously at every depth.

The general argument connects established results about braid signatures and quasimorphisms. The supporting materials also give a concrete three-strand word with 104 crossings at the third derived level. That finite example illustrates one case of the broader existence theorem.

The precise result

Let P_m be the classical disk pure braid group, with P_m^(0)=P_m and P_m^(k+1)=[P_m^(k),P_m^(k)]. For every m≥3 and every finite integer k≥1, some braid in P_m^(k) has standard oriented closure that is not integrally smoothly 1-solvable in the sense of Otto Definition 2.3.

Equivalently, the string-link concordance classes represented by P_m^(k) are not all in F₁^m. Since F_n^m⊂F₁^m for integers n≥1, this gives P_m^(n+2)⊄F_n^m for every m≥3 and integer n≥1, a negative answer to Question 3 in the Harvey–Park–Ray Oberwolfach contribution.

For the explicit third-derived example, set a=σ₁², b=σ₂², c=[a,b], d=a⁻¹ca, e=b⁻¹cb, u=[c,d], v=[d,e] and β=[u,v], using [x,y]=xyx⁻¹y⁻¹. The paper gives a 104-letter freely reduced Artin word for β with closure signature −2.

Why the result holds

The ordinary signature s of a three-strand braid closure has bounded failure of additivity. Its homogenization q is a homogeneous quasimorphism, exactly linear on powers. Published signature formulas show that q restricted to the pure braid group P₃ is not a homomorphism.

A nonhomomorphic homogeneous quasimorphism cannot vanish on a finite derived subgroup. Otherwise it would descend to a solvable, hence amenable, quotient, where homogeneous quasimorphisms are homomorphisms. The general ingredients are established results.

The ordinary signature and its homogenization are distinct. A suitable positive power is essential: nonzero q on a braid does not by itself give nonzero ordinary signature on that same braid. The powered braid has nonzero ordinary signature and zero pairwise linking numbers. A pointwise signature obstruction rules out an integral smooth 1-solution; adding split trivial strands reaches every m≥3.

The result uses the ordinary derived series of classical disk pure braid groups and integral smooth solvability of standard closures. It makes no claim for power subgroups, lower central series, rational derived series, surface braid groups, rational solvability or a merely topological solvability category.

The witness may depend on the finite depth k. No single braid in the intersection of all derived subgroups is asserted, and the explicit 104-crossing word is supplied only for k=3. No minimal crossing number or effective word-length bound at arbitrary depth is claimed.

For m=1 and m=2, the positive derived subgroups are trivial. The consequence for the solvable filtration is stated for integers n≥1; it does not contradict the prior n=0 containment discussed in the original report.

The general signature, quasimorphism and amenable-group tools are credited prior results. The contribution presented is their application to this particular containment question, together with the explicit finite example. No historical firstness, exhaustive novelty clearance or continued worldwide openness is claimed.

Failure of strong quadratic growth in unregularized sparse control of a critical wave equation

By Alec Kriebel, independent researcher.
Manuscript dated 14 October 2026 · Version 1.0 · Unrefereed preprint

Read the paper (PDF, 6 pages) · Source and supporting verification materials (ZIP) · Zenodo record

Plain-English explanation · Read on this page · Collaboration

Abstract

We give an explicit counterexample to retaining ordinary critical-cone strict positivity and strong control-L² quadratic growth after removing quadratic control regularization from the energy-critical quintic-wave problem of Kunisch and Meinlschmidt. On the three-dimensional unit ball, zero is the unique global optimizer for a sufficiently small positive pointwise control cap. Its ordinary critical cone is {0}, so the strict condition is vacuous, but feasible controls converging in L∞ have objective gap o(‖u‖²L²). Nearby radial terminal targets admit global optimizers, and every such optimizer has L² displacement divided by target displacement tending to infinity. Local L¹ quadratic growth survives. The construction realizes the established concentration and noncoercivity mechanism in the actual nonlinear source model, using classical wave estimates.

The idea in plain English

In optimal control, a control is an input chosen to make a system behave as desired. This paper studies a nonlinear wave equation, where the objective balances a desired final wave profile against penalties on the state and on the amount of control used.

A useful stability property says that moving away from the best control raises the objective by at least a fixed multiple of the squared distance. In this example, doing nothing is the unique global optimum, but increasingly short, small pulses have an objective penalty much smaller than their squared L² size. Uniqueness therefore does not supply that stronger growth property.

The striking feature is that the ordinary critical-cone test still holds: its cone contains only zero, so there are no nonzero directions on which the strict test can fail. The concentrating pulses reveal what this test misses. A weaker L¹ quadratic-growth estimate survives, and the paper also bounds how optimizers respond to nearby terminal targets.

The precise result

The model is the real defocusing quintic wave equation yₜₜ − Δy + y⁵ = u on the three-dimensional unit ball B, with zero position and velocity initially, homogeneous Dirichlet boundary conditions and final time 1. Let H=L²(B). Controls lie in L²(0,1;H) and obey ‖u(t)‖H ≤ ρ almost everywhere in time. There is ρ*>0 such that the conclusions hold for every fixed 0<ρ≤ρ* and every fixed finite ν≥0.

The objective Jd,ν retains one half of the squared terminal-position tracking error, one quarter of the fourth power of the L⁴(0,1;L¹²(B)) state norm, and the L¹(0,1;H) sparse-control penalty: γ=β₁=1. Only the quadratic control penalty is removed, β₂=0. The optional terminal-velocity term is ν‖yₜ(1)‖²H⁻¹(B)/2.

For target d=πe, with e the normalized first radial Dirichlet eigenfunction, zero is the unique global optimizer over all admissible controls. With A=‖u‖L¹(0,1;H), the objective gap Δ(u)=Jπe,ν(u)−Jπe,ν(0) satisfies Δ(u)≥A³/(12ρ²). The ordinary critical cone is {0}, so the strict substitute second-variation condition is vacuous. The cap threshold and this lower bound can be chosen independently of ν.

The actual nonlinear feasible pulses uₕ=he·1{|t−1/2|<h}, for 0<h<min(ρ,1/2), satisfy ‖uₕ‖L∞(0,1;H)=h, ‖uₕ‖²L²(0,1;H)=2h³ and Δ(uₕ)=(π²/3+2/π²)h⁴+O(h⁶). Strong control-L² quadratic growth therefore fails in both L² and L∞ neighborhoods of zero.

Global optimizers exist for every terminal target d∈H in this fixed small-cap setting. Along dε=(π+ε)e, as ε decreases to zero through positive values, every choice of global optimizers satisfies ‖uε‖L²/ε→∞. No uniqueness of perturbed optimizers is required.

Corollary 3 retains local weaker-norm growth: Δ(u)≥‖u‖²L¹/(4π²) for every admissible control with sufficiently small L¹ norm. For an arbitrary nearby target πe+w, put ε=‖w‖H. Every global optimizer, compared with the fixed zero optimizer, satisfies ‖u‖L¹=O(ε) and ‖u‖L²=O(√ε). The constants and this upper-bound neighborhood can be chosen uniformly over all finite ν≥0.

On the positive radial ray w=εe, every global optimizer satisfies ‖uε‖L¹=Θ(ε) and cε³ᐟ⁴≤‖uε‖L²≤C√ε for sufficiently small ε. The lower-comparison neighborhood may depend on the fixed ν. These bounds do not assert a sharp L² response exponent.

Why the result holds

Classical energy and Strichartz estimates make the nonlinear state close to the linear wave for small control mass: the state is O(‖u‖L¹), and the nonlinear remainder is O(‖u‖⁵L¹). This estimate is in a compatible energy-and-Strichartz state space; it does not assume that the nonlinear solution stays in one eigenmode.

The first eigenmode gives an explicit sine kernel for the terminal linear response. At the midpoint in time, the tracking gain exactly meets the sparse-control threshold. A cap-constrained moment estimate proves global optimality of zero, while pulses concentrating at that midpoint make the quadratic-growth quotient vanish.

The terminal tracking square also provides a weaker L¹ quadratic lower bound. A separate pulse comparison for perturbed targets yields the lower response bounds for every optimizer. These arguments use analytic estimates; the accompanying finite algebra checks are not a numerical solution of the nonlinear PDE.

Scope and limitations

This is a counterexample to retaining the ordinary critical-cone implication unchanged when the quadratic control penalty is removed. It does not rule out adapted sufficient conditions, enlarged cones, nondegeneracy assumptions or growth in weaker norms.

The ordinary critical cone is zero, so strict positivity there is vacuous. The result should not be described as a counterexample with a uniformly positive Hessian on every control direction.

The control cap is pointwise in time on the spatial L² norm. It is not a pointwise bound on |u(t,x)|. Here L¹ and L∞ mean time norms with values in L²(B), while control L² is the time-space L² norm. The state penalty remains present; “unregularized” refers to removing the quadratic control term.

The construction uses the three-dimensional unit ball, the defocusing quintic, zero initial data, a small positive cap and a particular target. It does not assert the same failure for every domain, every target, arbitrary large caps, Neumann conditions or boundary control.

The cap and base-target lower bounds can be chosen independently of ν. Upper target-response estimates and their neighborhood are uniform in finite ν; the radial lower-comparison neighborhood may depend on the fixed ν. No assertion concerns ν = ∞.

The response estimates compare optimizers with the fixed zero optimizer. They do not prove perturbed-optimizer uniqueness, a pairwise Lipschitz selection, L∞ convergence of perturbed optimizers, or a sharp exponent for the L² response.

The paper gives no certified numerical PDE constant or numerical value of the small-cap threshold. Its finite checks do not replace the analytic proof. The historical question and earlier mechanisms are attributed without a worldwide-firstness or present-day-openness claim.

The failure is specific to the selected target. For target d=0 in the same model, J0,ν(u)≥‖u‖L¹≥‖u‖²L²/ρ, so strong quadratic growth does hold. The theorem does not assert failure for all targets or all control caps.

Abstract

For every m≥3 and every finite k≥1, the kth ordinary derived subgroup of the pure braid group contains a braid whose standard closure is not integrally smoothly 1-solvable. Consequently P_m^{(n+2)}⊄F_n^m for every integer n≥1, answering negatively the derived-series containment question in the Harvey–Park–Ray Oberwolfach contribution. The proof combines established signature-quasimorphism results with amenable-quotient rigidity and a pointwise signature obstruction to 1-solvability. The general quasimorphism ingredients are prior results. An accompanying exact verification package also preserves an explicit 104-crossing example in P_3^{(3)}.

The idea in plain English

Pure braids return each strand to its starting position. Repeatedly taking commutators creates the derived series, an increasingly restrictive sequence of subgroups. A separate notion, called 1-solvability, asks whether the closed braid fits into a four-dimensional construction with specified surfaces and intersection properties.

The paper shows that for every number of strands at least three, a braid can lie arbitrarily far down the derived series and still fail 1-solvability. For each finite depth there is a witness; the argument does not use one braid that works simultaneously at every depth.

The general argument connects established results about braid signatures and quasimorphisms. The supporting materials also give a concrete three-strand word with 104 crossings at the third derived level. That finite example illustrates one case of the broader existence theorem.

The precise result

Let P_m be the classical disk pure braid group, with P_m^(0)=P_m and P_m^(k+1)=[P_m^(k),P_m^(k)]. For every m≥3 and every finite integer k≥1, some braid in P_m^(k) has standard oriented closure that is not integrally smoothly 1-solvable in the sense of Otto Definition 2.3.

Equivalently, the string-link concordance classes represented by P_m^(k) are not all in F₁^m. Since F_n^m⊂F₁^m for integers n≥1, this gives P_m^(n+2)⊄F_n^m for every m≥3 and integer n≥1, a negative answer to Question 3 in the Harvey–Park–Ray Oberwolfach contribution.

For the explicit third-derived example, set a=σ₁², b=σ₂², c=[a,b], d=a⁻¹ca, e=b⁻¹cb, u=[c,d], v=[d,e] and β=[u,v], using [x,y]=xyx⁻¹y⁻¹. The paper gives a 104-letter freely reduced Artin word for β with closure signature −2.

Why the result holds

The ordinary signature s of a three-strand braid closure has bounded failure of additivity. Its homogenization q is a homogeneous quasimorphism, exactly linear on powers. Published signature formulas show that q restricted to the pure braid group P₃ is not a homomorphism.

A nonhomomorphic homogeneous quasimorphism cannot vanish on a finite derived subgroup. Otherwise it would descend to a solvable, hence amenable, quotient, where homogeneous quasimorphisms are homomorphisms. The general ingredients are established results.

The ordinary signature and its homogenization are distinct. A suitable positive power is essential: nonzero q on a braid does not by itself give nonzero ordinary signature on that same braid. The powered braid has nonzero ordinary signature and zero pairwise linking numbers. A pointwise signature obstruction rules out an integral smooth 1-solution; adding split trivial strands reaches every m≥3.

Scope and limitations

The result uses the ordinary derived series of classical disk pure braid groups and integral smooth solvability of standard closures. It makes no claim for power subgroups, lower central series, rational derived series, surface braid groups, rational solvability or a merely topological solvability category.

The witness may depend on the finite depth k. No single braid in the intersection of all derived subgroups is asserted, and the explicit 104-crossing word is supplied only for k=3. No minimal crossing number or effective word-length bound at arbitrary depth is claimed.

For m=1 and m=2, the positive derived subgroups are trivial. The consequence for the solvable filtration is stated for integers n≥1; it does not contradict the prior n=0 containment discussed in the original report.

The general signature, quasimorphism and amenable-group tools are credited prior results. The contribution presented is their application to this particular containment question, together with the explicit finite example. No historical firstness, exhaustive novelty clearance or continued worldwide openness is claimed.

For the separate explicit example, the supporting derivation reconstructs the Goeritz form from crossing geometry and records a printed index discrepancy in Erle’s matrix formula. A separate Burau–Meyer calculation gives the same signature. This qualification concerns the finite example; the arbitrary-depth existence proof is independent of that calculation.

By Alec Kriebel, independent researcher.
Manuscript dated 14 October 2026 · Version 1.0 · Unrefereed preprint

Abstract

We give an explicit counterexample to retaining ordinary critical-cone strict positivity and strong control-L² quadratic growth after removing quadratic control regularization from the energy-critical quintic-wave problem of Kunisch and Meinlschmidt. On the three-dimensional unit ball, zero is the unique global optimizer for a sufficiently small positive pointwise control cap. Its ordinary critical cone is {0}, so the strict condition is vacuous, but feasible controls converging in L∞ have objective gap o(‖u‖²L²). Nearby radial terminal targets admit global optimizers, and every such optimizer has L² displacement divided by target displacement tending to infinity. Local L¹ quadratic growth survives. The construction realizes the established concentration and noncoercivity mechanism in the actual nonlinear source model, using classical wave estimates.

The idea in plain English

In optimal control, a control is an input chosen to make a system behave as desired. This paper studies a nonlinear wave equation, where the objective balances a desired final wave profile against penalties on the state and on the amount of control used.

A useful stability property says that moving away from the best control raises the objective by at least a fixed multiple of the squared distance. In this example, doing nothing is the unique global optimum, but increasingly short, small pulses have an objective penalty much smaller than their squared L² size. Uniqueness therefore does not supply that stronger growth property.

The striking feature is that the ordinary critical-cone test still holds: its cone contains only zero, so there are no nonzero directions on which the strict test can fail. The concentrating pulses reveal what this test misses. A weaker L¹ quadratic-growth estimate survives, and the paper also bounds how optimizers respond to nearby terminal targets.

The precise result

The model is the real defocusing quintic wave equation yₜₜ − Δy + y⁵ = u on the three-dimensional unit ball B, with zero position and velocity initially, homogeneous Dirichlet boundary conditions and final time 1. Let H=L²(B). Controls lie in L²(0,1;H) and obey ‖u(t)‖H ≤ ρ almost everywhere in time. There is ρ*>0 such that the conclusions hold for every fixed 0<ρ≤ρ* and every fixed finite ν≥0.

The objective Jd,ν retains one half of the squared terminal-position tracking error, one quarter of the fourth power of the L⁴(0,1;L¹²(B)) state norm, and the L¹(0,1;H) sparse-control penalty: γ=β₁=1. Only the quadratic control penalty is removed, β₂=0. The optional terminal-velocity term is ν‖yₜ(1)‖²H⁻¹(B)/2.

For target d=πe, with e the normalized first radial Dirichlet eigenfunction, zero is the unique global optimizer over all admissible controls. With A=‖u‖L¹(0,1;H), the objective gap Δ(u)=Jπe,ν(u)−Jπe,ν(0) satisfies Δ(u)≥A³/(12ρ²). The ordinary critical cone is {0}, so the strict substitute second-variation condition is vacuous. The cap threshold and this lower bound can be chosen independently of ν.

The actual nonlinear feasible pulses uₕ=he·1{|t−1/2|<h}, for 0<h<min(ρ,1/2), satisfy ‖uₕ‖L∞(0,1;H)=h, ‖uₕ‖²L²(0,1;H)=2h³ and Δ(uₕ)=(π²/3+2/π²)h⁴+O(h⁶). Strong control-L² quadratic growth therefore fails in both L² and L∞ neighborhoods of zero.

Classical energy and Strichartz estimates make the nonlinear state close to the linear wave for small control mass: the state is O(‖u‖L¹), and the nonlinear remainder is O(‖u‖⁵L¹). This estimate is in a compatible energy-and-Strichartz state space; it does not assume that the nonlinear solution stays in one eigenmode.

A cap-constrained moment estimate proves global optimality of zero, while pulses concentrating at that midpoint make the quadratic-growth quotient vanish.

The terminal tracking square also provides a weaker L¹ quadratic lower bound. A separate pulse comparison for perturbed targets yields the lower response bounds for every optimizer. These arguments use analytic estimates; the accompanying finite algebra checks are not a numerical solution of the nonlinear PDE.

This is a counterexample to retaining the ordinary critical-cone implication unchanged when the quadratic control penalty is removed. It does not rule out adapted sufficient conditions, enlarged cones, nondegeneracy assumptions or growth in weaker norms.

The ordinary critical cone is zero, so strict positivity there is vacuous. The result should not be described as a counterexample with a uniformly positive Hessian on every control direction.

The control cap is pointwise in time on the spatial L² norm. It is not a pointwise bound on |u(t,x)|. Here L¹ and L∞ mean time norms with values in L²(B), while control L² is the time-space L² norm. The state penalty remains present; “unregularized” refers to removing the quadratic control term.

The cap and base-target lower bounds can be chosen independently of ν. Upper target-response estimates and their neighborhood are uniform in finite ν; the radial lower-comparison neighborhood may depend on the fixed ν. No assertion concerns ν = ∞.

The response estimates compare optimizers with the fixed zero optimizer. They do not prove perturbed-optimizer uniqueness, a pairwise Lipschitz selection, L∞ convergence of perturbed optimizers, or a sharp exponent for the L² response.

The paper gives no certified numerical PDE constant or numerical value of the small-cap threshold. Its finite checks do not replace the analytic proof. The historical question and earlier mechanisms are attributed without a worldwide-firstness or present-day-openness claim.

The failure is specific to the selected target. For target d=0 in the same model, J0,ν(u)≥‖u‖L¹≥‖u‖²L²/ρ, so strong quadratic growth does hold. The theorem does not assert failure for all targets or all control caps.
